To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) The capacity of bone marrow to develop into mast cell progeny in vitro is genetically controlled.

(1) BM from certain strains of inbred mice produce large numbers of mast cell progenitors, (2) BM from other strains produce very few mast cell progenitors and (3) the genetic factors controlling the strain-response phenotype are predominantly background genome-associated.

the genetic factors determining the response of mouse bone marrow cells to culture conditions that promote mast cell development are predominantly associated with the non-H-2 genome and are not inherited as a single dominant trait.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of mast cells from pluripotential stem cells in the bone marrow of mice.
the genetic control of mast cell differentiation in vitro.
the genetic control of mast cell proliferation in vitro.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic factors, which are predominantly associated with the non-H-2 background, determine the capacity of mouse BM cells to develop into mast cell in culture.
the strain-dependent variation in mast cell development observed in bone marrow cultures is controlled by multiple genes, the expression of which is influenced by the H-2 complex.
the genetic control of mast cell response phenotype is complex, involving both the MHC and non-MHC regions of the genome, with a possible influence of the X chromosome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mast cell development in culture is controlled by multiple genes, some of which are linked to the MHC, others to other chromosomal loci.
genetic factors determine mast cell development from BM in vitro.

the genetic control of mast cell response phenotype is complex, involving at least two loci, one of which is closely linked to the MHC, and that these loci influence the capacity of the precursor cells to develop into mast cell and the capacity of the mast cells to proliferate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic influences on mast cell development in vitro are complex.
the genetic factors determining mast cell response phenotype are predominantly associated with the non-MHC background genome.
there are strain differences in the capacity of BM from inbred mice to produce mast cells under defined in vitro conditions.
